Field surveys of Caspian goby (Neogobius caspius) in the southern Caspian Sea have provided detailed morphometric data for this benthic species. The maximum total length observed across sampled populations reached 34.5 centimeters [Li = 34.5 centimeters], a dimension that distinguishes it from several smaller congeners inhabiting adjacent estuarine systems. Examination of reproductive anatomy revealed that the gonadosomatic index (GSI) attained a mean value of 13% [GSI = 13%] at 17.9 °C [T = 17.9 °C], a thermal regime typical of late spring spawning aggregations. This index reflects a moderate investment in gametic tissue relative to somatic mass, consistent with an iteroparous life history strategy among gobiids. Growth increment data derived from otolith readings further corroborated these length maxima, indicating that asymptotic size is approached gradually over several growing seasons.

Assessments of reproductive maturation in Neogobius caspius indicate that females achieve puberty at a total length of 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds well with the onset of vitellogenic oocyte development. The wet weight at puberty for an individual of this length was calculated as 10.7 grams [Wwp = 10.7 grams], a body mass that appears sufficient to support the energetic demands of initial gamete production. Comparisons with related species suggest that this pubertal size is relatively conservative, potentially reflecting adaptation to the specific prey base and thermal conditions of the southern Caspian basin. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from females measuring below this length consistently showed only pre-vitellogenic oocytes, confirming that 17 cm represents a reliable marker for the transition to reproductive potential. The length-weight relationship employed for these estimates was derived from local population samples.

The early life stages of Caspian goby are characterized by a particularly small size at emergence. Neonatal wet weight was determined to be 0.0007 grams [Wwb = 0.0007 grams], a figure based on the measured egg diameter of 1.1 millimeters and the assumption of near-spherical geometry. This minute birth mass places the species among the more fecund members of the family Gobiidae, as small egg size typically correlates with high fecundity and a planktonic larval phase. The newly hatched prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days post-eclosion. Field collections of yolk-sac larvae confirmed the presence of a substantial oil globule, which likely contributes to buoyancy and early energy provisioning. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs once the yolk is largely resorbed, typically within a week following hatching under ambient thermal conditions.

Adult female body mass in Neogobius caspius reaches an ultimate wet weight of 87.5 grams [Wwi = 87.5 grams] at the asymptotic length of 34.5 centimeters, representing the maximum somatic investment observed in reproductively mature individuals. This value was derived from the length-weight scaling relationship established for the population, which follows a power function typical of benthic fishes. In comparison, males tend to attain a slightly smaller ultimate mass, although sexual size dimorphism is not pronounced in this species. The 87.5 gram mass provides a substantial reservoir of somatic tissue that supports both maintenance metabolism and the energetic costs of repeated spawning events across multiple seasons. Field records of gravid females approaching this mass indicate they are capable of producing several thousand eggs per spawning event, underscoring the species' high reproductive output relative to its body size.

Longevity estimates for Caspian goby, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith age validation, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days] under natural thermal conditions averaging 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This corresponds to roughly six years, a relatively extended lifespan for a gobiid of moderate body size and likely reflects the stable, low-predation environment of deeper benthic habitats in the Caspian Sea. Senescent individuals collected during the final year of life show evidence of reduced gonadal investment and increased incidence of parasitic infestation. The age structure of wild populations typically exhibits a dominance of two- and three-year-old individuals, with progressively lower representation in older age classes. This lifespan places Neogobius caspius among the longer-lived members of its genus, potentially conferring resilience to interannual variability in recruitment success.
